locked_story.headline: THE MACHINE WITH NO DATASHEET
locked_story.one_line: On August 10th the National Science Foundation awarded the University of Alaska Fairbanks $324,995 for a fix to a problem that bites when a village puts a battery next to its diesel generator: two machines of about the same size, electrically close together, can start fighting each other and oscillate. The reason the standard remedies fail here is that nobody has an accurate model of the generator actually sitting in that powerhouse. So the proposal is to let the battery's own inverter put a question into the grid and listen to what comes back, learning the machine it has to live with. The award never once uses the word AI.
locked_story.story_question: How do you keep two machines from fighting when you have no idea how one of them behaves?
why_this_one: IN WINDOW: awarded 2026-08-10, three days old.

GENUINELY UNREPORTED: no outlet has covered it, and UAF's own news page carried a different, AI-branded grid award on August 11th while never mentioning this one. The 'unreported' claim is checkable and was checked against the UAF news index directly.
PRIMARY SOURCED: the NSF award record is the system of record, with award ID, dollar figure, dates, PI, program and full abstract. Nothing rests on a press release.
CONVERGENT: two researchers on two different beats found it independently and both recommended it first.

HONEST AI ANGLE: the mechanism is data-driven system identification and adaptive control, which is real machine learning and is the unglamorous kind that keeps lights on. The abstract calls it data-driven and never calls it AI, and that restraint is itself the most interesting fact in the story.

ALASKA-FIRST AND AI-FIRST: the stated payoff is lower energy costs and greater resilience for communities facing some of the nation's highest electricity prices. This is a story about Alaska possibly winning something.
DRAWABLE: the failure mode is two machines the same size, too close, ringing against each other. The fix is one of them asking a question out loud and listening. Both are pictures, not slides.

Different problem, different mechanism, different argument.

candidates.headline: NSF 2626692: the battery inverter probes the grid to learn the diesel generator nobody has a model for
Koniag Government Services wins a $63M ICE contract to run a 24-hour national law-enforcement call center
candidates.why_rejected: The AI content is an absence: the contract documents name database cross-checks, 'targeting focus and material', and a clause asking the vendor to identify 'emerging technologies'. No AI is named anywhere. That makes it a serious immigration-enforcement and Alaska Native corporation governance story with a thin technology spine, and this channel would be reaching to claim the AI. The cultural rules also bind hard here (an ANCSA corporation is not a tribal government and speaks for neither its shareholders' opinions nor Alaska Native people), and the contract record itself was one verification step away because usaspending.gov is JS-rendered. Genuinely newsworthy, wrong outlet, and it deserves better than an AI framing bolted on.

candidates.headline: Murkowski and Whitehouse introduce the Fisheries Science Modernization Act: eDNA stock assessment, and no algorithm in it
candidates.why_not: The strongest clean alternative and a genuinely good 'automation without an algorithm' story, well sourced across a senator's own release plus two independent Alaska outlets. It loses to the locked story on two counts: it was already covered by three Alaska outlets so the audience has seen it, and its AI content is entirely negative space. Carried forward as a strong future peg once a bill number is confirmed on congress.gov.
